idea_angle: Spring storm season guide to home repair scams: storm chasers, door-knockers, insurance claim tricks, deposits that vanish, and a step-by-step plan for hiring safely after damage.

script.title: After the storm: how home repair scams work, and how to hire safely
script.hook: 5 home repair scams show up after spring storms. Here's each one, and a 6-step plan to hire safely.

segments.heading: Why after storms
segments.narration: When a spring storm tears off shingles or drops a tree on the fence, two things happen fast. You need help, and you're stressed. That's exactly when home repair scammers arrive, sometimes from out of state, sometimes within hours. The FTC warns about them after every big storm. In this video, five scams you'll see after storm damage, and then a calm, step-by-step plan for hiring someone good, paying safely, and what to do if it's already gone wrong.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. the small round teal shield mascot with big curious eyes looking at a storm-damaged roof No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Door-knockers
segments.narration: Scam one, the door-knocker. A truck pulls up. 'We're working on your neighbor's roof, we noticed yours has damage too. We can start today.' Sometimes it's true that they're working nearby. But a company that finds you, rather than you finding it, deserves extra checks. Many are honest. Some are not licensed in your state, won't be around next month for the warranty, and use the pressure of 'today' to stop you comparing. You don't need to decide at the door. 'Leave a card, I'll call you' is a full answer.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a truck outside a row of houses No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The big deposit
segments.narration: Scam two, the big deposit. 'Materials are scarce after the storm, so we need half up front, in cash, to order them.' You pay, and the crew never comes back, or they do a day of work and vanish. Some deposit is normal on big jobs. But be wary of large amounts up front, cash only, or pressure to pay before there's a written contract. Pay in stages as work is completed, by check or card, so there's a record.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a stack of cash and an empty driveway No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Insurance tricks
segments.narration: Scam three, the insurance shortcut. 'We'll deal with your insurance company for you, just sign here.' That form may assign your insurance claim to them, so the money goes to the contractor, and you lose control over the work and the price. Another version: 'We'll cover your deductible.' That can be insurance fraud, and you're the one who signed the claim. Always talk to your own insurer first, and read anything with the word 'assignment' very carefully.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. an insurance form with a pen No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Fake inspectors
segments.narration: Scam four, the fake inspector. Someone says they're from the city, the utility, or FEMA after a big disaster, and that your home needs an urgent repair or an inspection fee. Real inspectors carry ID, and government agencies don't charge inspection fees at your door. Scam five, the free roof inspection that finds damage that wasn't there. Some dishonest inspectors create damage on the roof. If someone climbs up, ask to see photos, and get a second opinion.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a person with a clipboard on a roof No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Hiring safely
segments.narration: Now the safe plan. Step one, take photos of the damage and call your insurer. Step two, make temporary fixes only, like a tarp, and keep receipts. Step three, find contractors yourself, through neighbors, your insurer, or local listings with a real address. Step four, check each license with your state or city, and read reviews from more than one site. Step five, get at least three written estimates for the same work. Step six, a written contract with start and finish dates, materials, permits and warranty.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a numbered checklist on a clipboard No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Paying safely
segments.narration: On payment: agree a schedule tied to finished stages, and pay by check or card. Don't pay the final amount until the work is done, inspected if a permit needed it, and you're happy. Get lien waivers for big jobs, which show the contractor paid their suppliers. And if you signed a contract at your home, the FTC's Cooling-Off Rule may give you three days to cancel. The seller should tell you how. Check the FTC page for which sales it covers.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a progress bar with payments No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: If it went wrong
segments.narration: If you already paid someone who disappeared, report it to your state attorney general and local police, and to the FTC at report fraud dot F T C dot gov. Call your card company about a dispute if you paid by card. And be careful with anyone who calls offering to recover your money for a fee. Save this video for storm season, send it to a homeowner you know, and follow for one scam decoded every day.

script.title: After Tax Day: the scams that follow you (and what the IRS really does next)
script.hook: 6 tax scams start after you file, not before. Here's each one, and what the real IRS does next.

segments.heading: It's not over
segments.narration: You filed. Maybe you're waiting for a refund, maybe you owe, maybe you got an extension. Either way, you're still on the scammers' calendar, because after April fifteenth, people are expecting money or worried about penalties, and that's perfect cover. In this video, six scams that arrive after Tax Day, how each one works, and what the real IRS actually does next, so anything else stands out.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. the small round teal shield mascot with big curious eyes relaxing next to a filed tax return, then a phone buzzes No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Refund trackers
segments.narration: Scam one, the fake refund tracker. A text or ad says your refund is ready, just verify your details, or pay a small processing fee. The real tool is at I R S dot gov slash refunds. It asks for three things: your Social Security number or ITIN, your filing status, and your exact refund amount. No card, no bank login, no fee. Most e-filed refunds arrive within weeks. If yours is late, the tool tells you, and if the IRS needs to verify your identity, it sends a letter.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a fake site next to a simple form No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Penalty texts
segments.narration: Scam two, the missed-deadline text. 'You failed to file by April fifteenth. Pay your penalty now to avoid wage garnishment.' The IRS doesn't text about penalties. If you really did file late and owe tax, there can be failure-to-file and failure-to-pay penalties, but you'll hear about them in a letter, and see them in your online account. If you missed it, file as soon as you can, even if you can't pay. That keeps penalties smaller.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a phone with a red final notice No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Fake audit letters
segments.narration: Scam three, the fake audit letter. It arrives by mail, looks official, says you underreported income, and gives a phone number to call within ten days. The phone number goes to the scammer. Check any letter by looking up its notice number on I R S dot gov's 'understanding your notice' page, signing in to your online account to see whether it's there, and calling the IRS on a number from I R S dot gov. Real notice? Respond calmly by the deadline. Fake one? Report it to TIGTA at tigta dot gov.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a letter with a circled phone number No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Payment lookalikes
segments.narration: Scam four, the payment lookalike. People who owe search 'pay IRS', click an ad, and land on a site that charges big processing fees or simply takes the card number. Start at I R S dot gov slash payments. Direct Pay from your bank is free; card processors listed there charge a fee. And if you can't pay the full amount, look at payment plans on the same site, before you call any 'tax relief' ad. The FTC warns some relief companies charge large fees up front.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a search result with a fake badge No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Preparer problems
segments.narration: Scam five is about the person who did your taxes. If a preparer promised a bigger refund, took a percentage of it, or didn't sign the return, look at it again now. The IRS reminds people they're responsible for what's on their return, even if someone else prepared it. Inflated credits can mean a bill later with interest and penalties. If something looks wrong, an amended return and a reputable tax professional can fix it before the IRS asks.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a return with a magnifier No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Identity theft
segments.narration: Scam six is quieter: identity theft. If your e-filed return was rejected because one was already filed with your Social Security number, or you get a letter about a return you didn't file, someone used your identity. Follow the steps in the IRS identity theft guide, file Form 14039 if told to, and freeze your credit. Then get an IRS Identity Protection PIN, so it can't happen next year.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a shadowy figure holding a tax form No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Your checklist
segments.narration: Your after-Tax-Day checklist. One, check refunds only at I R S dot gov slash refunds. Two, ignore texts and emails about penalties and refunds. Three, look up any letter's notice number before you call anyone. Four, pay only from I R S dot gov slash payments. Five, keep a copy of your return. Six, get an IP PIN for next year. Send this to whoever handles the money in your house, and follow for one scam decoded every day.

idea_angle: How one hacked email account leads to many: the takeover chain, the warning signs, a 20-minute lockdown, and a recovery plan if it already happened. Spring-clean framing with an affiliate disclosure for password managers.

script.title: How 1 hacked email unlocks everything (and how to lock it in 20 minutes)
script.hook: 1 hacked email can unlock 10 other accounts. Here's how it happens, and a 20-minute lockdown.

segments.heading: The master key
segments.narration: If you only protect one account this year, make it your email. Not your bank. Your email. Because almost every 'forgot password' link on the internet goes to your inbox. So whoever controls your email can reset your bank login, your shopping accounts, your social media, sometimes your phone account. In this video, how the takeover chain works, the warning signs, a twenty-minute lockdown you can do tonight, and what to do if it already happened.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. the small round teal shield mascot with big curious eyes holding a big key shaped like an envelope No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: How the chain works
segments.narration: Here's how it usually goes. First, the password leaks. Maybe it was in a data breach on another site where you used the same one. Maybe you typed it into a fake sign-in page from a scary email. Second, they sign in, often quietly, and add a rule that hides security alerts. Third, they click 'forgot password' on your other accounts, and the reset links land in the inbox they now control. Fourth, they change your recovery phone so you can't get back in, and message your contacts for money.
segments.on_screen_text: Leak → sign in → reset → lock out
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. dominoes falling from an envelope No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Warning signs
segments.narration: Warning signs it's happening: password reset emails you didn't ask for. Security alerts about a new sign-in from a city you've never been to. Friends asking about a weird message you didn't send. Emails missing, or in folders you didn't create. Or you suddenly can't sign in at all. If you see any of these, don't wait. Go straight to the lockdown steps, from the app or by typing the address, not from a link in an email.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a phone with alert notifications No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Password
segments.narration: Lockdown step one: a new password for your email that you use nowhere else. Long beats clever, so four or five random words is great. If remembering unique passwords for everything sounds impossible, that's what a password manager is for. It creates and remembers them, and you remember one strong master password. There are good free ones. Our comparison is linked in the description, with the affiliate disclosure, and Bitwarden's free plan is a fine start.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a vault with many keys No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Two-step
segments.narration: Step two: turn on two-step sign-in. Then a stolen password alone isn't enough. Text message codes are better than nothing. An authenticator app is better. Passkeys, which sign you in with your face, fingerprint or device PIN, are even harder to phish. Pick one and turn it on tonight. And a rule for all of them: never read a code to anyone who contacts you. Nobody legitimate needs it.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a phone with a lock and a fingerprint No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recovery and rules
segments.narration: Step three: check your recovery phone number and recovery email are current and yours. Step four: look in your email settings for forwarding rules and filters you didn't create, and delete them. Step five: look at the list of devices signed in, and sign out of any you don't recognise. These three take about five minutes and close the doors a hacker leaves open behind them.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a settings page with toggles No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The rest
segments.narration: Now spring clean the rest. Change passwords on your bank, phone carrier and main shopping accounts so each one is unique, and turn on two-step there too. Then close accounts you don't use any more. Download anything you want to keep first. An account that doesn't exist can't be hacked, and it can't be used to phish you with a 'your account will be deleted' email.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a broom sweeping old account icons No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Already happened
segments.narration: If it already happened: try the account's official recovery page, from the app or typed address. Once you're back in, change the password, turn on two-step, remove rules and unknown devices, and warn your contacts by another route. Then change passwords on accounts that use that email. The FTC has a step-by-step guide to recovering a hacked email or social account. Send this to someone who still uses one password everywhere, and follow for one scam decoded every day.

script.title: Moving this spring? Rental listing scams and moving company scams, decoded
script.hook: 2 big moving scams hit every spring: the fake rental and the hostage mover. Here's how to spot both.

segments.heading: Moving season
segments.narration: Spring and summer are moving season, and moving is expensive, rushed and stressful, which is exactly what scammers look for. Two scams cause the most damage. The fake rental, where you pay a deposit for a home that isn't available, or isn't theirs to rent. And the dishonest mover, who quotes low, loads your things, then demands much more to deliver them. In this video, how both work and the checks that beat them.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. the small round teal shield mascot with big curious eyes surrounded by moving boxes No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The fake rental
segments.narration: The fake rental starts with a listing that's a little too good: a great place, a great price, a quick reply. Often the photos are copied from a real listing. The 'landlord' is out of the country or too busy to show it, but you can drive by and look through the window. They ask for an application fee, a deposit and the first month's rent, by payment app, wire or crypto, before you've been inside or signed a lease. Then they stop answering, and sometimes the same home was 'rented' to five people.
segments.on_screen_text: Too good + can't see it + pay first
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a pretty house with a for-rent sign and a shadow No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Rental checks
segments.narration: The checks. Search the address and the photos online; if the same place appears under another name or price, walk away. See the inside, in person or with someone you trust, before paying anything. Confirm who owns it, with the county property records or the real property manager. Sign a lease before paying. And pay by check or card, not wire, gift card, crypto or a payment app to a stranger. The FTC is clear: anyone who wants money before you've seen the place or signed a lease is a red flag.
segments.on_screen_text: See it · check owner · lease first
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a magnifier over a listing No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Lowball movers
segments.narration: Now movers. The first trap is the lowball quote, given over the phone or online without anyone looking at your stuff. It's cheap because it isn't real. Another version is a broker, not a mover, who takes a deposit and passes your job to whoever is cheapest. FMCSA, the federal agency that oversees interstate movers, lists red flags: no in-person or video estimate, a big cash deposit, no physical address, and a company name that changes.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a quote sheet with a tiny number No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Hostage loads
segments.narration: The worst version is the hostage load. They pack your truck, then announce the price has doubled because of 'extra weight' or 'extra services', and they won't deliver until you pay. Your furniture, photos and paperwork are somewhere in a warehouse. This is why the estimate and the paperwork matter so much. For interstate moves, you should get a written estimate, and the mover must give you FMCSA's rights and responsibilities booklet.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a locked truck with boxes inside No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Check a mover
segments.narration: How to check a mover in ten minutes. For interstate moves, look up their USDOT number on the FMCSA site and check they're registered as a mover, not just a broker. For local moves, check your state's licensing. Read complaints, not just stars. Get at least three in-home or video estimates. Make sure the estimate is in writing, with the company's full name and address. And don't pay a large deposit, especially in cash.
segments.on_screen_text: USDOT check · 3 estimates · no big deposit
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a laptop with a lookup page No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Moving day
segments.narration: On moving day: don't sign a blank or incomplete document. Make sure the bill of lading matches what you agreed. Keep valuables, medicines and important papers with you. Take photos of furniture before it's packed. And keep every receipt and message.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a clipboard and a phone camera No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: If it went wrong
segments.narration: If a mover is holding your things, or a rental deposit vanished: for interstate moves, file a complaint with FMCSA. Report to your state attorney general and to the FTC at report fraud dot F T C dot gov. If you paid by card, call the card company about a dispute. script.title: Older Americans Month: the 7 scams that target older adults most
script.hook: 7 scams target older adults more than anyone, and each 1 has a simple rule that beats it.

segments.heading: Why this month
segments.narration: May is Older Americans Month, and this video is for older adults and the people who love them. Scams hit every age, but some are built specifically for older adults: people who answer the phone, are polite to strangers, and have savings. Being targeted isn't about being less sharp. These are professional criminals with scripts. So here are the seven scams that target older adults most, one simple rule for each, and how families can help without taking over.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. the small round teal shield mascot with big curious eyes sitting with an older adult and a cup of tea No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Family emergency
segments.narration: Number one, the family emergency. A crying grandchild, or a 'lawyer' or 'police officer', says there's been an accident or an arrest and money is needed today, often in cash collected by a courier. Voices can now be cloned with AI from a short video clip. The rule: hang up and call the family member, or their parent, on the number you already have. And agree a family safe word that a caller must say.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a phone with a crying emoji No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Government imposters
segments.narration: Number two, government imposters. Social Security says your number is suspended. The IRS says there's a warrant. Medicare says your card is expiring and they need your number. The rule: real agencies don't call to threaten you, don't suspend Social Security numbers, and never want gift cards. Hang up and call the agency on its official number.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. an official seal with a red cross No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Bank fraud call
segments.narration: Number three, the bank fraud department. The caller ID shows your bank. They say there's suspicious activity and ask you to read back a code, or move your money to a 'safe account'. The rule: your bank will never ask for that code, and there is no such thing as a safe account. Hang up and call the number on the back of your card.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a bank card and a phone No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Tech support
segments.narration: Number four, tech support. A pop-up says the computer is infected and to call Microsoft, or a caller says they're from Apple. They ask for remote access, then often fake a refund mistake and ask for money back. The rule: real warnings never give a phone number to call, and you never let a stranger control your computer.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a red warning screen No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Romance
segments.narration: Number five, romance. A widower on an oil rig, a doctor overseas, a soldier. Weeks of kind messages, then a need for money: customs fees, a medical bill, or an investment opportunity. The rule: never send money, gift cards or crypto to someone you've only met online, no matter how real it feels.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a heart with a dollar sign No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Prizes and funerals
segments.narration: Number six, prizes. You've won millions, just pay the taxes first. The rule: if you have to pay to get a prize, it's a scam. And number seven, the scams that follow a death in the family: calls about a loved one's 'debts', or a funeral home imposter. The rule: family members generally aren't responsible for those debts, and you call the funeral home on a number you already have.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. a giant check and a candle No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: How families help
segments.narration: For families, the best protection is a relationship, not a lecture. Set up a call-me-first rule. Put the bank's number and yours by the phone. Help turn on 'silence unknown callers'. Check in about scams the way you'd check in about health. If money has gone, call the bank first, then the National Elder Fraud Hotline at one eight three three, three seven two, eight three one one. Our large-print pack for seniors is in the bio; it's our own product. Share this with someone you love.
